**Vision-Based Desktop Automation with Dynamic Icon Grounding**  
**Lorelei Lee Lopez**

**Objective:**

The goal of this project is to create a Python application that can locate and open the Notepad icon on a Windows desktop no matter its location on the screen, using computer vision. This will be done by taking a screenshot and searching within the screenshot using a text description of said icon. This program will not rely on a saved image for reference. For this particular assignment, the Notepad icon will be the targeted icon, however it can be used for locating and opening other icons as well.

**Assumptions:**

* Windows 10/11 using a resolution of 1920x1080 with 100% scaling, on a single monitor.   
* A Notepad shortcut exists on the desktop and is visible.  
* Internet Access to connect with: JSONPlaceholder API and Claude API with a valid API key.  
* Icon size and position will vary.  
* Desktop theme can vary between light and dark mode.  
* Unforeseen pop-ups may appear

**System design:**

When the program begins, first it will fetch the first 10 posts from the API. Next, for each post that was fetched, it will take a screenshot of the desktop and search for the Notepad icon using a text description of the icon. Once the icon is located it will double-click the icon and wait for it to open. Once it is open it will paste in the blank note “Title:{title}\\n\\n{body}” in the text area. Next, it will save it as post\_{id}.txt in the tjm-project folder, and close the Notepad. This is repeated from a fresh screenshot for the next post. 

![][image1]

**Grounding strategy:**

To better understand why a grounding strategy is necessary to locate an icon on the screen, first it is necessary to understand where a vision model lacks. A vision model will run into difficulty locating an icon due to a few reasons:

* Screen vs icon size: Icons are often very small in comparison to the desktop size they sit in, as that gap widens, accuracy falls.  
* Screenshot limitations: Depending on the size of the screenshot it may be required to be scaled down in order to be appropriately ingested by the model. This shrinking will further decrease icon size and cause finer details to be lost.  
* Clutter: Icons, such as Notepad, do not exist alone, desktops can be filled and become cluttered with various icons including similar looking ones.

Based on “ScreenSpot-Pro: GUI Grounding for Professional High-Resolution  
Computer Use” by Li et al, a grounding strategy can help mitigate these drawbacks and increase accuracy of locating the intended icon. This can be accomplished using similar steps with a few changes for the scope of this project:

* Handling pop-ups: Before beginning its search the planner will evaluate if a pop-up is blocking the desktop. If there is, it will find the safest approach to proceed whether that is to close the pop-up and search, or report back an error.  
* Inference: The planner model, in this case Claude, would look at the screenshot and the description of the icon and start looking in the most likely location of where the icon could be in addition to looking near other elements or icons that it may typically reside near. Oftentimes, neighboring elements can be easier to spot than the intended icon target to help point the model in the right direction.  
* Simplified scoring: The planner model returns candidate regions and ranks them by likelihood of containing the icon. It searches them in descending order. The paper instead scores each region using the grounder's predictions and merges overlapping regions. I rank by the planner's judgment alone.   
* Recursive search: The highest scoring candidate is cropped and searched again by zooming in so the icon takes up more of the image until the intended icon is found or it has searched the area and not found anything.  
* Coordinates: When the intended icon is located the grounder points to where it is on the cropped screenshot and then returns the coordinates on the full screenshot to show location on the screen.  
* Verify: The verifier now with the coordinates, decides if this is the target, if the target is somewhere else, or if it is not found. If it is not found it will move on to the next highest scoring candidate. When the icon is found it will return the (x,y) coordinates needed to locate the icon. If every candidate fails, the program stops, saves a debug screenshot, and reports an error instead of guessing 

For this particular project Claude will be used as the planner, grounder and verifier. Each will have separate prompts and Sonnet 5.5 with medium effort will be used. This is a different approach to the paper referenced above which used GPT-4o as the planner and OS-Atlas-7B as the grounder. Because Claude is not a dedicated pointing model  the search zooms in until the icon fills much of the crop, and the verifier confirms the icon before the program clicks. I chose this setup because of my constraints: the time limit, the tools readily available, token use, and the limits of my laptop. 

**Alternatives and Tradeoffs:**

Other simpler methods could be used to search for an icon. However while they excel in simplicity they lack flexibility.

* Matching the exact icon image: Icons can vary in size, theme, and more. This would require a pre-saved copy of the icon image ahead of time thus it would not allow for the program to be used across different desktops or if the desktop theme changed.  
* OCR: If the label is not available or is using a different name, it would be unable to locate the icon across different desktops.  

The approach chosen for this project is intended to work across various desktops, unlike the above two alternatives, it will be slower, cost money, and can fail due to the model making mistakes. This is why the verification step exists to help decrease the chances of that happening. However, those drawbacks can be improved upon in later iteration with more time and resources while still maintaining use across desktops.

**Error Handling:** 

* Icon not found: If the verifier has checked every candidate and is unable to locate the intended icon the program will stop, save a debug screenshot and report the error.  
* Wrong or similar-looking icon: If the verifier detects that the icon shown is not the intended icon it will reject the candidate and move on to the next candidate.  
* Coordinate off screen: If the program detects that the coordinates suggested are outside of the screen or cropped screenshot it will reject it as well.  
* Connection issues: If the program is unable to connect to the internet or API, it will try again and if it is still unable to connect it will report the error.

**Future Improvements:**

For a future iteration the program could remember the last location and use that as a starting point for the next time. This would be used as a hint to try and improve speed. Each loop would still use a fresh screenshot and verify the result, this would just be to try and cut down on the amount of search steps needed.
